lesson.title: Two Reactive Elements, Twice the Slope: The Second-Order Filter
lesson.summary: A second-order filter contains two independent energy-storing elements, giving it a steeper 40 dB per decade roll-off than a first-order filter and, depending on damping, the ability to peak near its cutoff, the mechanism behind band-pass and band-reject filters.
lesson.body:
A second-order filter contains two independent energy-storing elements, typically one inductor and one capacitor in an RLC circuit, and is governed by a second-order differential equation, the class of circuit covered in Second-Order Circuits. Its transfer function has two poles instead of one, and that second pole changes the filter's behavior in two important ways.

First, the roll-off steepens. Far from cutoff, a two-pole response falls off in proportion to the square of frequency rather than frequency itself, which in decibels means the attenuation grows at 40 dB per decade, twice the rate of a First-Order Filter, because each pole contributes its own 20 dB per decade and the two stack. Second, unlike a first-order filter, which can only fall off monotonically away from its passband, a second-order filter can peak near its resonant frequency if it is lightly damped, high Q, which is precisely the mechanism that makes Band-Pass Filter and Band-Reject Filter circuits possible: both require two reactive elements working together to create that resonant peak or dip.

Consider a maximally flat, Butterworth-style, second-order low-pass filter, whose magnitude response is |H(f)| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)⁴), the exponent 4 reflecting its two poles. Evaluate it one decade above cutoff, at f = 10fc: (f/fc)⁴ = 10⁴ = 10,000, so |H| = 1/√(1 + 10,000) = 1/√10,001, about 1/100.005, approximately 0.0099995. In decibels, 20 log10(0.0099995) is about minus 40.0 dB, exactly double the minus 20 dB per decade you calculated for a first-order filter at the same one-decade offset, confirming the 40 dB per decade rate.
